scope: Literal candidate only, with source and context consulted for fidelity and recurrence.

tell_ledger.evidence: No first person appears. “Maybe you’d rather” tentatively describes a reader preference and does not invoke author authority.
The entire candidate is one tentative preference, with no commands, sequence of lessons, questions, or compressed conditions.

The preceding context discusses support from peers and community; the dating heading then makes a lover as another possible source of support relevant. The complication is prepared by that live topic.
There is no scene and no series of scene beats that could map to source obligations.
“A lover” is the relationship under discussion, not a convenient prop introduced to carry successive teaching jobs.
“Support” refers to the help just described from peers and community. It does not masquerade as a concrete personal incident or replace a lived account that this opening needs to provide.

“Maybe” preserves uncertainty about whether the reader has this preference; it is not hesitation staged between multiple argumentative beats. “As well” preserves the additive relationship from source.
No concrete image is introduced, and no follow-up translation or moralization appears in the candidate.
A single opening sentence offers no series of equally weighted, efficient teaching units. It tentatively raises a wish rather than compressing several requirements.
The sentence offers no permission formula or counseling requirement. It leaves open whether the reader wants a lover's support.

Although it transitions to dating, it makes a substantive connection: someone receiving support might want it from a lover as well. It is tied to the preceding support discussion rather than announcing a generic next section.
There is no taxonomy, matched opposition, or balanced set of cases. “As well” adds a possibility without closing a category system.

The sentence notices a plausible wish arising inside the preceding discussion: support may be wanted from a romantic partner. There is no run of outline slots to which it could be reduced, and no reason to add a counterexample to this isolated opening.
No material is reordered within this sentence. Its placement after a discussion of sources of support is intelligible without appealing to detector avoidance.
“Support person were” changes to “support came from” to remove a specific referent problem after the Hearthwork peer. The otherwise retained words are ordinary and do not show synonym churn.
There is no negative-reveal contrast or “not X, it is Y” formula.
“Maybe” and “you’d rather” keep this a possible preference, not a completed principle or thesis about relationships.
No premise is followed by a sentence knocking it down. Only one tentative proposition is present.
The sentence does more than announce dating as the next topic: it identifies a possible reason the reader would want that relationship in this discussion of support.
The ending “as well” is an ordinary source-retained addition, not a clever closer, antithesis, or polished punch line.
One finite preference construction contains one complement about support from a lover. There is no coordinated series of argumentative jobs.

The two second-person forms are “you’d” and “your.” They identify whose possible preference and support are at issue. The sentence issues no instruction or generalized reassurance and does not perform a sequence of coaching moves.
No scenery or invented relatable incident appears. The lover is a possible relationship category, not a faux personal detail.
No question, self-answer, faux secret, or suspense device appears.
No colon or dramatic reveal appears.

“Support” repeats the section's subject in order to carry the reader from peer/community support into romantic hopes. That recurrence supplies the precise relation being repaired rather than restating a completed lesson.
None of the listed Joel tic words or specified metaphorical uses appears.
This is an opening about a possible preference, not a section ending on healing, reassurance, summary, or uplift.
The candidate is the first sentence of a longer paragraph. It introduces a thought; it does not append a summary to a thought completed one sentence earlier.
The inner child is not named, and “the kid” does not occur.

“Your support” now denotes the support being discussed. “A lover” introduces an indefinite possible source, so the just-described Hearthwork peer is no longer implicitly designated as the person who should become a lover. “As well” reads additively in the surrounding discussion of multiple sources of support.
There is no first-person claim about Joel or any invented biographical statement.
There is no named entity, cited study, product, or external factual claim. The tentative preference is preserved from source.
